name: The Sophists as a social and professional class
plain_explanation: The word 'Sophist' originally just meant something like our word 'professor': a paid teacher who taught wealthy young men practical skills, especially the skills needed to win in law courts and assemblies.
precise_definition: A class of professional itinerant teachers in fifth-century Greece who, in the absence of public education, taught for a fee the sons of those with private means, chiefly the arts of argument and oratory useful in the law-courts and political life, without founding schools, brotherhoods, or esoteric doctrines as other philosophical traditions did.
why_it_mattered: The Sophists' social position (paid teachers of the rich, unattached to religious or communal traditions) explains both their popularity with one class and their deep unpopularity, later amplified by Plato, with another, and it marks a new, secular model of intellectual life distinct from the quasi-religious philosophical schools that preceded them.
historical_origin: Arose from the practical demands of Athenian legal and political life, in which litigants argued their own cases before large panels of ordinary citizen-judges chosen by lot.
examples: Athenian litigants hiring Sophists to write speeches or teach forensic skill
Protagoras's alleged fee arrangement tied to his student's first legal victory
objections: Plato devoted himself, in Russell's view unfairly, to caricaturing and vilifying the Sophists.
The general public viewed them with hostility rooted partly in class resentment and traditionalism.
competing_positions: The older model of a philosophical school as a quasi-religious brotherhood with common life and esoteric doctrine, which the Sophists explicitly lacked
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell compares the Sophists' social role to that of modern corporation lawyers, who similarly serve the interests of a wealthy class through specialized argumentative skill.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Tied to Athenian democracy's legal system and to class conflict between the cultured rich and the traditionalist, envious poor.
